summary: Jade Vault is a markdown vault in the style of Obsidian with an AI agent called Jade built in. It runs as one page in a browser and as an Android app.
The vault is a virtual file system. Jade is a loop: your message plus a prompt built from her steering files, memory and skills goes to a model, she may call tools, and she answers.
The model is not part of the app. You point it at Ollama, Ollama Cloud, Groq, OpenRouter, llama.cpp or any OpenAI compatible server.

keyPoints: Jade Vault is a markdown vault with a built-in agent, as one browser page or an Android app.
The vault is the shared ground; Jade is a model driven loop around it.
You choose the model: local Ollama, Ollama Cloud, Groq, OpenRouter, llama.cpp or any OpenAI style endpoint.
Around the loop sit memory, autonomy, world tools, integrations and safety.
Anything that runs on its own is off until you switch it on.
Her settings and work products are ordinary files in the vault.

items: ELI5. Imagine a big box of notes with a helper living inside. You write notes, the helper reads them, remembers them, and can do chores for you when you ask.

Imagine a notebook that can think. You keep notes in it, and a helper called Jade lives inside, reads them, writes new ones, runs small programs, and remembers what you told her last week. That is Jade Vault in one sentence.

It is built from a few pieces. The vault is a virtual file system, the shared ground. In a browser it is stored in IndexedDB, and in the Android app it is a real folder called JadeVault. Jade is the agent. She is not a program that thinks by herself.
She is a loop that sends a prompt to a model and runs the tools the model asks for.

items: Because the model lives outside the app, you decide who answers. You can use Ollama on your own computer, Ollama Cloud, Groq, OpenRouter, llama.cpp or any server that speaks the OpenAI format, and you can add a chain of fallbacks.
On the phone the network is native, so local Ollama needs no special browser setting.

Around the loop sit five kinds of capability. Memory keeps facts, a journal and a search index. Autonomy lets her wake on schedules, a heartbeat or her own curiosity. World tools give her the camera, the phone, the screen, a second browser and SSH on Android.
Integrations connect MCP servers, an HTTP API, messengers and mini apps. Safety is approvals, secrets and labels on untrusted text.
Two rules run through the whole design. First, the vault is the memory and the interface: what steers her is a plain file she can read and mostly write.

Second, everything risky is gated: secrets are placeholders, calls and texts ask you first, and external text is labelled as data, not instructions. This course follows those ideas one chapter at a time, and each lab rebuilds a small piece in Python.

A note on versions. The course follows the repository at version 2.28.1. The documentation was written across many releases, so some pages name an older version. When a feature has a version, it is mentioned.

chapters.title: Notes and the vault
summary: Notes are markdown files. A link to another note is written in double square brackets, and an embed, such as an image, puts an exclamation mark in front. Tags start with a hash sign.
The notes screen shows backlinks, a graph, a reader and a split editor. Obsidian style scripts and Templater templates are supported inside a sandbox.
Her own files live under /Jade. The labs classify files, find links and build backlinks.

keyPoints: Links are [[Note]]; an alias is [[Note|text]]; a heading link is [[Note#Heading]].
Images and notes embed with ![[photo.png|300]].
Backlinks list the notes that point at the current note.
Templates use <% tp.date.now() %> style code from Templater.
Note scripts (dataviewjs) run in a sandbox: they read the vault, with no network and no file changes.
Jade's files, such as /Jade/SOUL.md and /Jade/Memory.md, are ordinary notes.

items: ELI5. A note is a page in a folder. A double-bracket link is a string tied between two pages, so you can walk from one to the other and back.
A vault is a folder of markdown notes that link to each other. Jade Vault shows the notes in a tree, with search, an editor and a reader. The links between notes become a graph you can look at.
A link is two pairs of square brackets around a note name. After a vertical bar you can put the text to display, and after a hash sign a heading in the target.
A note that has an exclamation mark in front is an embed: it shows the note or image inside the page, for example an image with a width of 300. Tags are words that start with a hash sign.

# Trip planning

See [[Lisbon]] and [[Maya|my friend Maya]].
Heading link: [[Budget#Flights]].

items: Because links are plain text, a backlink is easy to compute: look through every note and keep those that link to this one. The app does this for you, and a shell command called backlinks does too. The same text files can also be read by scripts and by Jade.

Two Obsidian style features are included. Dataview style note scripts, in blocks marked dataviewjs, can query the vault, for example a table of notes with a tag. Templater templates, kept in the Templates folder, insert text such as the date or the current title.
Both run in a sandbox that reads the vault but cannot use the network or change files.

Jade keeps her own files in a folder named Jade. The file SOUL.md is her persona, AGENTS.md holds your standing instructions, Memory.md holds durable facts, and skills, flows and playbooks have their own folders. Since they are ordinary notes, you can read, edit and back them up like anything else.

chapters.title: A turn, step by step

maps.title: Turn
links: Prompt | is built from | Steering and memory
Tool results | return to | The model
Loop | repeats | Until a plain reply

summary: A turn begins when a message arrives. The harness builds a prompt, calls the model, runs any tools the model asks for, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model answers without a tool call.
The system prompt is built in a fixed order from the base text, SOUL.md, AGENTS.md, memory and the skill list. Before each call the context guard checks the whole request fits in the model's window.
A limit on tool rounds stops a runaway loop. She tells you when it stopped, and you can send continue.

glossary.def: Call the model, run its tools, repeat.
The standing instructions placed before the chat.
A request from the model to run a named tool with arguments.
One model call that asks for tools, plus running them.
The setting that limits tool rounds per message.
How much text the model can read at once.

keyPoints: send(text) records the message with a timestamp, runs any slash command, then runs the agent loop.
The system prompt joins base or SYSTEM.md, SOUL.md, AGENTS.md files, the memory block, the skill list and tool text.
Before each call, the harness may prefetch memory hits and matching skills.
A tool error becomes an Error result that the model can react to.
The loop ends on a reply with no tool calls, a user abort, or maxTurns rounds.
Messages you type while she works are queued and added before her next model call.

items: ELI5. A turn is like a short conversation round: tidy the desk, read the question, ask the brain, use a tool if needed, and answer.
A turn is everything between your message and her final answer. The harness, which is the code around the model, does the same steps every time. That regularity is what makes an agent debuggable.

Step one is the request. The system prompt is assembled: the built-in intro and guidelines, or your SYSTEM.md instead, then SOUL.md, then your AGENTS.md files, then the memory block, then the list of skills and the text about tools.
After that comes the chat history, and a summary if old turns were compacted.

lesson.code:
1. record message (timestamp), run slash command
2. compact old turns if needed
3. prefetch memory hits and matching skills
4. build request: system prompt + history + tool schemas
5. fit the context (compact or trim, learn real limits)
6. call the model, streaming
7. run each tool call, add results as tool messages
8. repeat from 3 until a reply has no tool calls

items: Step five is easy to forget. The harness estimates the whole request, not just the chat, and shrinks it if it will not fit. If the server still says the prompt was too long, the guard learns the real limit and remembers it for next time.

Failures are part of the loop. If a tool fails, the result is the text Error plus the reason, and the model sees it and can try again. If the provider fails with a network, rate limit or server error and you set fallbacks, the harness switches provider and retries the round.
Finally there are limits. The setting maxTurns caps the tool rounds, and if it is reached she says she stopped after that many rounds and you can send continue.
Everything fetched from the web or SSH is wrapped with a label saying it is data, not instructions, so that a web page cannot give orders to the agent.

chapters.title: Tools, gating and safety

maps.title: Tools
links: Switch | removes | A pack of tools

summary: Jade has about thirty tools: notes, shell, node, Python, SQLite, web, MCP, flows, schedules and more. On Android there are packs for senses, phone, screen, a second browser and SSH.
A tool exists for the model only if the pack switch allows it and any special condition holds. Each pack shows its context cost, because tool descriptions take room in the prompt.
Secrets are written as {{NAME}} and filled in outside the model, and risky actions ask you first.

glossary.def: The description of a tool and its arguments that the model sees.
A group of tools with one switch, like phone or browser.
A {{NAME}} that is replaced by the real value after the model writes it.
A dialog that asks you before an action runs.
Text from outside, labelled so it is not read as instructions.
Model Context Protocol: a way to plug in more tools.

keyPoints: Tools are listed to the model only when their switch and conditions allow.
Each pack in Settings → World shows how much context it costs.
Secrets are placeholders like {{NAME}}; the real value is added outside the model and echoes are redacted.
Calls, texts, SSH commands, new playbooks and restore ask you first.
Web pages, SSH output and screen text are labelled as data, not instructions.
During a curiosity wake her tools are filtered, so she cannot reach phone or Sentry unless you widen it.

items: ELI5. Tools are the helper's hands. You decide which hands she may use, and secret keys are kept in your pocket, never shown to her brain.

A tool is a function with a name and a description of its arguments. The model sees the description and may ask for the tool by name. Everything useful Jade does goes through tools, so the tool layer is also where safety lives.
Not every tool is always offered. A switch in Settings, World, can remove a whole pack, such as the browser or phone tools, from her prompt. A pack that is off costs no context and cannot be used.
A few tools also need a condition, for example the skill search tool only exists when the skill router is active.

The risky capabilities are guarded in layers. Calls and texts ask you first, and emergency numbers are never dialled. SSH commands ask you, with credentials that she never sees. A new or changed playbook needs your approval before it can run unattended.
Restoring a backup is something only you can do.

Secrets work in a clever way. When Jade writes an API call, she writes a placeholder such as double braces around a name. The harness replaces it with the real key after the model's output, outside the model.
If the key later appears in a result, it is redacted back to the placeholder, so it does not leak into chats or logs.

Prompt injection is the other big risk. A web page, an SSH output or the text on the screen could contain a sentence like ignore your instructions. Jade Vault wraps all such text with a plain label that says it is data, not instructions, and tools that return it say so every time.

Finally, some settings she cannot edit at all: the numbers that a Sentry flow may contact, the hourly limit and the consent switches. If an agent could change its own safety limits, they would not be limits.

chapters.title: Memory, search and context

maps.title: Memory
links: Hybrid search | fuses | Keywords and meaning

summary: Jade remembers in layers: a Memory file of durable facts that goes into every prompt, a journal entry per chat, your notes, the raw chats, and a vector index that makes all of it searchable.
Search is hybrid. It runs keywords and meaning at the same time and merges the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion. If the embedder is missing, it falls back to keywords and then BM25.
When a chat grows too long, old turns are compacted into a summary so the request fits the model's window.

glossary.def: A file of durable facts, one bullet per line, added to every prompt.
A short entry for each chat, saved under /Jade/Journal.
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text.
A ranking function: term frequency times inverse document frequency, with length normalisation.
Reciprocal rank fusion: merging ranked lists by adding 1 over (k plus rank).
Replacing old turns with a short summary.

keyPoints: Memory layers: Memory.md, journal, notes, raw chats and a vector index.
The index is /Jade/.index/vectors.db, an ordinary SQLite file that is a cache you can delete.
A search runs FTS5 keywords and vector nearest neighbours, then fuses them with RRF.
BM25 rewards rare query words that appear often, and normalises for document length.
Auto-compaction runs after a number of turns or when the last answer filled too much of the window.
The /context command shows where the window goes.

items: ELI5. Memory is a diary the helper can search two ways: by exact words, and by meaning. Then she blends both lists into one best list.

A language model forgets everything between calls, so the harness builds memory around it. The first layer is a file. Memory.md holds durable facts, one bullet per line, such as the user's name or preferences, and it is injected into every prompt. Because it is a note, you can read and edit it.

The second layer is the journal. When you leave a chat or it gets compacted, a short entry is written to a dated note, and any new durable facts are copied to Memory. Raw chats are also stored with timestamps and tool calls, and a tool can read and search them.

Finding things uses an index. Jade Vault keeps a SQLite file with a full text index and a vector index. A search asks both. The keyword side finds the exact words. The vector side finds notes with a similar meaning, using embeddings from a model such as nomic-embed-text through Ollama.
The two lists are merged by reciprocal rank fusion.
BM25 is the classic keyword score. A document scores higher when it contains a query word often, when that word is rare across all documents, and when the document is not very long.
RRF is simpler: each list gives a document points of one over a constant plus its rank, and the points add up, so a document that ranks well in both lists wins.

Context is the other half. The window of a model is limited, and tools alone can take about ten thousand tokens at full load. A guard estimates the size of the whole request, compacts old turns into a summary, then trims bulky tool results, and learns real limits from errors.
The slash command context shows where the room goes.

maps.title: Skills
links: Skill | is | A folder with SKILL.md
Description | decides | When it is used

summary: A skill is a folder under /Jade/skills with a SKILL.md file. The file starts with frontmatter that has a name and a description, then the instructions. Jade loads a skill on demand with the skill tool.

Listing every skill costs context. With fifteen or fewer, all are listed. With more, only the six best for the current message are listed, chosen by meaning and whole word overlap, and a search tool finds the others.
The description is all the router sees, so write it as when to use the skill, in the words a user would say.

glossary.def: A reusable procedure written as a SKILL.md file.
The block between --- lines with name and description.
Code that picks which skills to list for a message.
A tool that searches the skills that were not listed.
Dropping weak matches: far in meaning and no shared words.
A built-in skill that teaches Jade to write new skills.

keyPoints: A skill folder is /Jade/skills/kebab-name/ with SKILL.md and optional files.
Run one with the skill tool or /skill:name.
Up to 15 skills are all listed; with more, the best 6 are listed.
Ranking fuses vector meaning with whole word overlap.
Strict mode drops a match with a vector distance over 0.6 and no word overlap.
Write a description that says when to use the skill; put the procedure in the body.

items: ELI5. A skill is a recipe card. She keeps the best few cards on the table and can look up the rest in the drawer when needed.

A skill is a recipe card. It tells Jade how to do one kind of job, such as filing an invoice or writing an atomic note, in steps. Because it is a plain file, anyone can write one, and you can share it by copying the folder.

lesson.code:
---
name: invoice-filing
description: Use when the user wants an invoice saved, renamed and linked to its project note.
---
# Steps
1. Read the invoice and find the date, supplier and total.
2. Rename the file to YYYY-MM-DD-supplier.
3. Link it from the project note.

items: The trouble is context. Every skill name and description in the prompt costs tokens, and a vault can have dozens of skills. The router solves this. With fifteen or fewer, it lists them all.
With more, it scores each against the current message, lists only the best six, and gives Jade a find_skill tool for the rest.

The score blends two signals. One is meaning: embeddings of each skill's name and description in a skills collection of the vector index. The other is overlap of whole words. In strict mode a match that is far away in meaning, with a distance over 0.6, and shares no words is dropped.
Counters keep track of how often each skill was offered, found and used.

This is why the description matters so much. It is the only text the router sees. Say when to use the skill in the words a person would say: use when the user wants an invoice saved. Do not put the procedure in the description. One skill should do one job.

Jade can also write skills. A built-in skill called skill-creator teaches her how, and the built-ins include daily review, atomic notes, a literature note, and math notes. Skills are the cheapest way to change her behaviour without changing the app.

chapters.title: Running on her own: heartbeat, schedules and curiosity

maps.title: Autonomy
links: Schedule | runs | Prompt, shell or flow
Reward | is | Measured from the vault

summary: Everything that runs without you is off until you switch it on, runs only while the app is alive, and is logged. The heartbeat reads a checklist file every N minutes and answers HEARTBEAT_OK when nothing needs attention.
Schedules run a prompt, a shell command or a flow, written in plain English or as cron. Command and flow schedules run without the model.
Curiosity wakes her at random times to explore, reflect, connect notes, practice, anticipate, ask a question or rest. It scores activities by learning progress, so noise earns no bonus.

glossary.def: A periodic check driven by HEARTBEAT.md.
The silent answer when nothing needs attention.
A job that runs a prompt, a shell command or a flow at a time.
Five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.
How much a forecast error is falling over time.
A random source that stays unpredictable and so teaches nothing.

keyPoints: Heartbeat: every N minutes (default 30) inside active hours; an empty checklist skips the model call.
Schedules accept plain English like every weekday at 9am, cron, or @daily.
Command and flow schedules log to /Jade/Logs/cron.log and notify on failure.
Curiosity: a window (default 08:00 to 22:00), a daily cap (default 5) and a steering file CURIOSITY.md.
Learning progress is the slow error average minus the fast one, never below zero.
Reward is measured by diffing the vault; her self-score cannot exceed the measured value by more than 0.2.

items: ELI5. Heartbeat is a gentle tap every half hour asking, is anything to do? If the list is empty she goes back to sleep without bothering the brain.
An assistant that only answers when you ask is useful. One that can also check things by itself is more useful, and riskier.
So the autonomy features share rules: they are off until you turn them on, they run only while the app is open or kept alive in the background on Android, and each run is logged.

The heartbeat is the simplest. Every N minutes inside the hours you allow, Jade reads a note called HEARTBEAT.md, which is your checklist, and follows it. If nothing needs attention she answers HEARTBEAT_OK, and that run is silent and pruned.
If the file has only comments, headings and empty checkboxes, the run is skipped without even calling the model.

Schedules are time based. You write when in plain English, such as every weekday at 9am, or in cron, or with a shortcut like @daily. A schedule can run a prompt through Jade in a chat, or a shell command, or a flow.
The last two do not need the model, so they are cheap and run on their own, with output in a log file and a notification on failure.

Curiosity is the unusual one. At random times in a window you choose, Jade wakes in her own chat and picks an activity from a menu: explore, reflect, connect notes, practice a skill, anticipate something you may need, ask you one question, or rest.
A file called CURIOSITY.md steers her with topics and things to avoid.

The suggestion is scored by learning progress, an idea of Schmidhuber's. Each activity has a small forecaster of how rewarding it will be. Progress is the slow average of the forecast error minus the fast average, never below zero.

An activity whose results stay random keeps a high but flat error and earns no bonus, which avoids the noisy TV trap. The reward itself is measured, not claimed: the harness compares the vault before and after, counting new notes, changed notes, links and memories.

summary: A flow is an n8n style automation kept as JSON in /Jade/Flows. It is a list of steps that run in order, and each step's output becomes $json for the next step.
Step types include Tool, JavaScript, Shell, Decide, Ask AI, Jade agent, Note, Set fields, If, Switch, For each, Wait, Notify, Run flow and Stop. Text fields may hold double-brace expressions.
A flow starts by hand, on a schedule, or when a note changes, and each run is logged step by step.

glossary.def: A saved list of steps, run in order.
The output of the previous step, available to the next.
What starts a flow: by hand, a schedule or a note change.
A step that picks one option and returns probabilities.
Running a failing step again, up to three times.
JavaScript inside {{ }} in a text field, run in a sandbox without network.

keyPoints: Flows are JSON files /Jade/Flows/NAME.flow.json.
Each step's output is $json for the next; other names are $input, $node["Step"], $vars, $item, $index, $now and $today.
Steps can retry 0 to 3 times or continue on error.
Triggers: by hand, a schedule (every weekday at 9am, cron, @daily), or a note or folder change.
Flows also run from the shell (flow run), scripts (jade.flow), the API and Jade's flow tool.
Every run is logged with each step's input, output and time.

items: ELI5. A flow is a row of boxes joined by pipes. Each box does a job and passes its result to the next, and you can see where it got stuck.

A flow is a small program built from boxes. The first box reads a note, the next decides something, the next writes a result. You can build one in the Flows tab, or ask Jade to build it, and it is saved as a JSON file in the vault.

lesson.code:
{"name": "Inbox triage", "trigger": {"type": "note", "path": "/Inbox.md"}, "steps": [
  {"type": "note", "name": "Inbox", "action": "read", "path": "/Inbox.md"},
  {"type": "each", "items": "$json.split('\n').filter(l => l.startsWith('- '))", "steps": [
    {"type": "decide", "name": "Urgent?", "state": "{{ $item }}", "question": "Is this urgent?", "kind": "yesno"},
    {"type": "if", "condition": "$json.result === true", "then": [
      {"type": "note", "action": "append", "path": "/Urgent.md", "content": "- [ ] {{ $item }}"}]}]},
  {"type": "notify", "title": "Inbox triaged"}]}

items: Data moves through the steps like water through pipes. The output of one step is called $json in the next. You reach it inside any text field with double braces, such as {{ $json.name }}.
Other names are available: the input of the flow, the output of a named step, variables, the loop item and its index, and today's date.

Steps do many things. A Tool step calls any of Jade's tools. A JavaScript step runs code in a sandbox. A Shell step runs a command. A Decide step asks a small decision model and returns the winner with a confidence and probabilities. An Ask AI step gets one answer.
A Jade agent step runs a full chat turn. There are also If, Switch, For each, Wait, Notify, Run flow and Stop.

Flows can fail, so each step can retry up to three times or continue on error. Every run is logged with the input, output, log and time of each step, so you can see exactly where it went wrong. A flow that fails sends a notification when it ran from a schedule.

Flows start in several ways: by hand, on a schedule, or when a note or folder changes. They can also be called from the shell with flow run, from scripts with jade.flow, over the HTTP API, and by Jade herself with the flow tool.
Because command and flow schedules need no model, a flow is the right tool for anything that should simply happen the same way each time.

chapters.title: Playbooks: deterministic automation

maps.title: Playbooks
links: Approval | binds | A hash of content

summary: A playbook is Jade's version of Ansible: a saved JSON list of tasks that call any tool, the browser or built-in actions, in the same order each time, with no model in the loop.

Tasks have a do action and keywords such as when, loop, register, retries, until, failed_when, ignore_errors, block, rescue and always. Strings may hold double-brace expressions in a small safe language.
You approve a playbook when it is saved, and again whenever its content changes, so a schedule or flow can run it unattended.

glossary.def: A saved JSON list of tasks run without a model.
One action with arguments and keywords.
A keyword that stores a task's result in a variable.
Tasks that run when a block fails.
A fingerprint of the playbook; a change makes it unapproved.
A safe mini language for when, until and templates.

keyPoints: Chat is for exploring and deciding; a playbook is for repeating.
Playbooks live in /Jade/Playbooks/NAME.json and are edited in the Playbooks tab.
The expression language has no JavaScript: only variables, literals, operators and listed functions.
An undefined name is an error, not an empty string.
At most 1000 tasks and 300 seconds per run (maximum 900).
Only an approved, unchanged playbook runs from a flow or a schedule.

items: ELI5. A playbook is a fixed recipe with no thinking: do step one, then two. You sign it, and if anyone changes a word it needs your signature again.

When Jade explores, she reasons. When something must happen the same way every time, reasoning is a risk. A playbook removes the model from the loop. It is a list of tasks, each a tool call with fixed arguments, so the same input gives the same steps.

lesson.code:
{"description":"Price of the lamp","allow_hosts":["shop.example"],"vars":{"max":50},"tasks":[
 {"name":"Open the shop","do":"browser.goto","url":"https://shop.example/lamp"},
 {"do":"browser.extract","css":".price","register":"price"},
 {"do":"assert","that":["price | float <= max"],"msg":"too expensive: {{ price }}"},
 {"do":"save","path":"/Jade/Playbooks/out/lamp.txt","value":"{{ today() }} {{ price }}","append":true}]}

items: If you know Ansible, the keywords will look familiar. The keyword when skips a task if its expression is false. Loop repeats over a list. Register stores a result in a variable. Retries and until repeat a failing task. Failed_when turns a success into a failure. Ignore_errors keeps going.
A block groups tasks, rescue runs on failure and always runs either way.

The expression language is a small safe interpreter. It has numbers, strings, lists, comparison and logic operators, in, is defined, and a list of filters such as float, which strips currency symbols so that the text $12.50 becomes 12.5. It never runs JavaScript.
A name that is not defined is an error rather than silently empty, which catches typos before they cause damage.

Approval is what makes unattended runs safe. When you save a playbook from the tab, you approve it, and the approval is tied to a hash of its content. If anyone changes the file, the hash changes and the playbook is no longer approved until you approve it again.
A flow or schedule will refuse to run a playbook that is new or changed.

More limits protect you. The allow_hosts list limits where the browser may go and which URLs any task may fetch. Run variables are limited to the ones the playbook declares. Saves go only under /Jade/Playbooks/out.
A failure stops the run at that task unless you wrote ignore_errors or a rescue, and nothing is repaired or guessed.

chapters.title: The knowledge graph

maps.title: Knowledge
links: Verdict | is | Proven, contradicted or unknown
Open world | means | Missing is not false

summary: The knowledge graph holds facts such as works_at(alice, acme), rules that derive new facts, and constraints that must never be broken. A Datalog reasoner, written in Rust and run as WebAssembly, checks claims against them.
Every answer is one of three: proven with its proof, contradicted, or unknown. The graph is open-world: something missing is not false.
Facts Jade adds are proposed until you confirm them, so you decide what counts.

glossary.def: A relation between things, like works_at(alice, acme).
A statement that derives new facts: head :- conditions.
A pattern that must never match, written with a leading !.
The engine that derives facts and checks claims.
Assuming unknown things might be true, not false.
The facts and rules a conclusion rests on.

keyPoints: Facts live in /Jade/Knowledge/facts.jsonl and rules in /Jade/Knowledge/rules.dl.
Rules use variables that start with a capital letter: above(X, Z) :- reports_to(X, Y), above(Y, Z).
A constraint such as ! one_employer: works_at(P, A), works_at(P, B), A != B. flags any match.
Verdicts are proven, contradicted (the opposite holds or a constraint would break) or unknown.
Confirmed facts are yours; proposed ones wait for you; rejected ones can never be added again.
A graph of 180,000 derived facts took about 0.15 s in the browser's tests.

items: ELI5. A knowledge graph is a wall of true little sentences with string between the names. It can tell you yes, no, or I do not know.

A knowledge graph stores knowledge as small statements. A fact says a relation holds between things, for example works_at with alice and acme. Rules let the graph work out more facts. If bob reports to alice and carol reports to bob, then a rule about above can conclude that carol is above alice.

lesson.code:
works_at(alice, acme)
reports_to(bob, alice)
reports_to(carol, bob)

above(X, Y) :- reports_to(X, Y).
above(X, Z) :- reports_to(X, Y), above(Y, Z).

! one_employer: works_at(P, A), works_at(P, B), A != B.

items: Constraints say what must never happen. The line starting with an exclamation mark says that a person may not work at two different places. If two facts match it, the graph reports a contradiction and shows the facts involved.
Running Check over notes that Jade turned into facts is a way to find where your own notes disagree.

A question gets one of three answers. Proven means the claim follows from the facts and rules, and the proof is shown. Contradicted means its opposite holds, or accepting it would break a constraint. Unknown means nothing says either way.
That last answer is important: the graph is open-world, so a missing fact is not treated as false.
The reasoner is Datalog, a small logic language that always terminates and is fast. It is written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, so it runs in the page.
Two rules keep it sound: every variable in a rule head or comparison must appear first in an ordinary condition, and a relation cannot depend on its own absence round a loop.
The graph is under your control. Facts you add are confirmed. Facts Jade adds are proposed, and a proof that rests on a proposed fact says so. If you reject a fact, Jade cannot add it again.
With Verify answers on, she checks the factual claims in her own answers against the graph and marks each with a tick, a cross or a question mark.

chapters.title: Autonomous mode and plans

maps.title: Autonomy
links: Critical path | sets | The finish date

summary: In autonomous mode Jade works through a queue on her own, the way an operating system schedules programs: interrupts first, then a priority queue with aging, then round robin with feedback for long goals.
You set the limits: steps per hour, a daily cap, quiet hours, a pause while you use the app, and approval for tools that reach outside the vault. Everything is logged.
Plans are Gantt charts for projects with dependencies, milestones and a critical path.

glossary.def: Jade works through her queue without being asked, within your limits.
An urgent item that goes first.
Raising a waiting task's priority so it is not starved.
Giving each long goal short turns in rotation.
A bar chart of tasks over time.
The chain of tasks that sets the finish date.

keyPoints: Tier 1 interrupts go first in arrival order; Jade may hold at most 3 of her own.
Tier 2 orders by priority 0 to 100, plus up to 40 for waiting, plus 10, 30 or 50 for a deadline within a day, an hour or already passed.
Tier 3 gets slices of 2, 4 or 8 steps; a goal that uses its slice drops a level, one that waits 30 minutes rises one.
Tier 3 gets every 4th turn when tier 2 also has work.
Each slice ends with STATUS: done, continue or blocked.
Defaults: 60 steps an hour, 600 a day, quiet hours 11pm to 7am.

items: ELI5. Autonomous mode is a to-do tray with rules: urgent things first, waiting things get bumped up, big jobs get short turns, and she sleeps at night.

If you have ever waited for a slow computer, you have met a scheduler. An operating system must decide which program runs next. Jade Vault applies the same idea to an agent's to-do list. In Schedule, Queue, a switch called Autonomous lets her work through it without you.

The queue has three tiers. Tier one is interrupts: urgent items that go first, in arrival order, with at most three that Jade herself may hold. Tier two is a priority queue for one-off work. Each task has a priority from 0 to 100, and waiting raises it by up to 40, so nothing waits forever.
A deadline within a day adds 10, within an hour adds 30, and one that has passed adds 50.

Tier three is round robin for long goals. A goal gets a short slice of 2, 4 or 8 model steps depending on its level. A goal that uses its whole slice drops a level, and one that waited 30 minutes rises one.

When tiers two and three both have work, tier three gets at least every fourth turn, so long goals never starve. Between slices she keeps only a short note, and each slice ends with a status line: done, continue or blocked.
Limits keep this safe. She stops in quiet hours, which start at 11pm and end at 7am at first, and when the step budget for the hour or day is used. She pauses while you use the app or chat.

Tools that reach outside the vault, such as phone, SSH, browsers and MCP servers, wait for your Allow button for that one task. Stop turns it all off at once, and every action is logged to /Jade/Autonomy/log.md.

Plans are for work that takes weeks. Under Schedule, Plans shows a project as a Gantt chart with a bar per task, arrows for dependencies, diamonds for milestones and a line for today. The critical path is the chain of dependent tasks that sets the finish date, drawn with a bright edge.
Dragging a bar moves the tasks that depend on it.

Plans and the queue are separate, with one link. With autonomous mode on and the setting to work on her ready plan tasks, each of Jade's tasks whose dependencies are done becomes a tier three goal, and finishing it marks the plan task 100 percent.

chapters.title: Think, delegate and the model router

maps.title: Think
links: think | builds | A tree of thoughts
Router | picks | A model per message

summary: The think tool searches a tree of reasoning lines and checks each with something that can say no, such as running code or checking a file. The best verified line is the answer.
A failed check from a real verifier is a veto, not an average, so a confident judge cannot rescue a solution that fails its test.
The delegate tool runs a sub-agent with a clean context and returns one report. The model router chooses a quick or strong model for each message.

glossary.def: Branching several lines of reasoning and keeping the best checked ones.
A check, such as running code, that can reject a thought.
A failure that cannot be averaged away.
Keeping only the top few nodes at each depth.
A sub-agent that works in its own clean context and reports back.
A decision model that picks which of your models answers.

keyPoints: think verifiers: code (read-only JavaScript), file, rubric and an independent judge.
Search modes are beam (default), best_first and puct, with budgets in nodes, seconds and tokens.
Trees are saved after each step and episodes are logged.
delegate is read-only by default, with 8 steps (max 15) and 120 s (max 300), and its report is capped at 6000 characters.
A delegate cannot nest or run twice at once.
The router uses the decision model to send everyday chat to a quick model and hard questions to a strong one.

items: ELI5. Think is trying a few ideas and testing each one with something that can say no, like running the code. A failed test cannot be talked around.
Models often answer with confidence and are wrong. The think tool is a cure based on checking.

Instead of one answer, Jade tries several lines of thought, and each line is checked by something that can say no: a test that runs, a file that must exist, a rubric of yes or no items, or an independent judge.

The design document ranks verifiers in tiers. Tier one is executable ground truth, such as running code and checking the result. It can veto. A solution that fails its test does not get partial credit from a judge that likes it.
Lower tiers are scored, and the model grading itself is the weakest, with its weight capped.

A node's score is the weighted average of its checks, where each weight also counts how reliable that verifier has proved to be. When a line reaches a result, a credit step finds which thought mattered most, using generalised advantage estimation, an idea from reinforcement learning.
Search is beam by default because a phone can only afford about ten to forty node checks, too few for statistics-heavy methods.

The delegate tool is a different kind of help. It starts a small second agent with a clean context, lets it read, search and fetch for a few steps, and returns one short report. The pages it read never fill Jade's own context. By default it is read-only.
It cannot call itself, and its report is framed as data.

The model router is a third. Before each message, the decision model, which can be a local model through Ollaya or Ollama, picks which of your models should answer. Everyday chat goes to a quick one and a hard request goes to a strong one.
This saves time and cost, and you configure it under Decision models.

practice.title: Advantages
practice.intro: Write advantages(rewards, values, gamma, lam): for steps t from 0, delta_t = r_t + gamma*V_(t+1) - V_t, where V after the last step is 0. A_t = delta_t + gamma*lam*A_(t+1), with A after the last step 0. Return the list of A_t rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Work backwards from the last step.
practice.solution:
def advantages(rewards, values, gamma, lam):
    n = len(rewards)
    out = [0.0] * n
    nxt = 0.0
    for t in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        v_next = values[t + 1] if t + 1 < n else 0.0
        delta = rewards[t] + gamma * v_next - values[t]
        nxt = delta + gamma * lam * nxt
        out[t] = round(nxt, 4)
    return out

chapters.title: Jade Lisp and scripting

maps.title: Lisp
links: Jade Lisp | is | A small Lisp

summary: Jade Lisp is a small Lisp in the style of Scheme and Clojure, part of the base system. It builds small languages for rules and workflows, and scripts that call Jade's tools.
Programs can run in a sandbox with only the verbs you give them and a step limit called fuel, so a program written by someone else cannot read files, call tools or loop forever.
Scripts in node can also use a jade object: jade.tool, jade.ask, jade.decide, jade.flow, jade.shell, jade.notify and a key value store.

glossary.def: A language where code is lists, written with parentheses.
Code that writes code; defmacro with quasiquote.
A domain specific language: a small language for one job.
A limit on evaluation steps that stops runaway programs.
A place where a program can use only the functions you give it.
A script call that runs any of Jade's tools.

keyPoints: Data: numbers, strings, symbols, :keywords, lists, maps, nil, #t and #f.
Forms include define, lambda, let, if, cond, while and defmacro; tail calls run in constant space.
(tool/NAME :arg value) runs any tool; jade/ask, jade/flow, jade/shell and jade/notify are also available.
pure=yes runs a whole program without tools, files or JavaScript; fuel=N limits steps.
Three ways to build a DSL: macros, a sandbox, or parsing the text as data.
In node: await jade.tool(name, args), jade.ask(prompt), jade.decide({...}), jade.flow(name, input), jade.kv.

items: ELI5. Lisp is a tiny language written in nested brackets, small enough for a helper to run safely with a limit on how long it may work.
A Lisp program is a tree written with parentheses. The first item in a list is the function and the rest are its arguments, so adding two numbers is written plus, one, two inside parentheses.
It looks odd at first, but it has a great advantage: code and data have the same shape, so programs can easily write and inspect other programs.

lesson.code:
(define square (lambda (x) (* x x)))
(square 5)                ; => 25

(define fact
  (lambda (n) (if (< n 2) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1))))))
(fact 5)                  ; => 120

;; calling Jade's tools from Lisp
(tool/notes_search :query "Lisbon")
(jade/notify "Done" "The report is ready")

items: Jade Lisp has the usual forms: define, lambda, let, if, cond and loops with named let, plus macros written with defmacro and quasiquote. It adds maps with keywords, try and catch for errors, and tail calls that run in constant space, so a loop does not grow the stack.

Every tool is callable from Lisp as tool slash name, with keyword arguments. That makes it a good scripting language for chains of tools, and for small languages. There are three ways to build a DSL. With macros, the new language is Lisp with new words.
In a sandbox, you give the language its verbs as plain functions and run a program written by someone else where only those verbs exist. Or you can parse the text as data and walk the forms yourself.

The sandbox is the safe choice for untrusted programs, such as one from a note or another model. The program cannot read files, call tools or loop forever, because you also give it a step limit called fuel. The option pure=yes runs a whole program with no tools, files or JavaScript at all.
Outside Lisp, the node scripts in the shell, in a flow's JavaScript step and in Jade's own bash, have a jade object.

A call such as jade.tool with a name and arguments runs a tool, jade.ask gets one model answer without a whole chat, jade.decide asks the decision model, jade.flow runs a flow, and jade.kv keeps small values between runs.
Files that a script writes are visible to the tools it calls, and the other way round.

chapters.title: Connect, back up, secure and build

maps.title: Connect
links: HTTP API | answers | JSON over GET

summary: Jade Vault connects outward in several ways: an HTTP API on the phone, MCP servers, the Vector and Discord messengers, webxdc mini apps, and a fleet broker that shares one vault between devices.
A scheduled backup uploads a compressed, optionally encrypted file to your own server. Jade can start one but she cannot restore.
The app is built by applying ordered exact-match patches to a base page; if a patch does not match, the build fails loudly.

glossary.def: An optional phone-side server that answers GET requests with JSON; off by default.
A secret sent in the Authorization header to prove access.
Sandboxed offline mini apps in a zip with index.html.
Messengers where Jade can be a bot, through small bridge servers.
One shared vault on a small server used by phones and browsers.
A replacement whose old text must occur exactly once, or the build stops.

keyPoints: The API is off by default; every call except /v1/health needs the token.
/v1/chat?message=TEXT sends a message that also appears in the app; errors are JSON with HTTP 400, 401, 404, 409, 502 or 504.
A backup is JSON, gzip, then optionally AES-GCM with a PBKDF2 key of 210,000 rounds; the server checks a SHA-256 header.
Backup names use only letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore and end in .json or .json.gz.
Webxdc apps are sandboxed with no vault access and no network.
npm run build makes dist/jade-vault.html; npm test runs dozens of Playwright suites; the APK needs a JDK, not the Android SDK.

items: ELI5. You can reach the helper from outside by a door with a key, keep spare copies of the box locked on your own shelf, and the app is built by careful find-and-replace.

A personal agent is more useful when it can be reached. Jade Vault has several doors, and each is a switch that is off until you turn it on. The HTTP API lives in the Android app. When enabled, it listens on your chosen port and answers GET requests with JSON.
A message sent to the chat endpoint goes through the normal chat and appears in the app.

lesson.code:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "http://PHONE:8787/v1/chat?message=What%20notes%20mention%20Lisbon%3F"

# errors are JSON too: {"ok":false,"error":{"code":"busy","message":"..."}}
# 400 bad request  401 token  404 unknown chat  409 busy  502 model error  504 still working

items: Other doors include MCP servers, configured in a file, that plug in more tools. The Vector and Discord bridges let Jade act as a bot, with roles: the owner gets the full Jade, admins get extra powers, and everyone else gets friendly chat.
Webxdc apps, such as the built-in Jade Link messenger, are small sandboxed apps that can exchange updates with her but cannot see your vault or the network.

Backups protect your data. A scheduled backup uploads to a server you run. The file is JSON, compressed with gzip, and optionally encrypted with AES-GCM using a key derived with PBKDF2 at 210,000 rounds.

The server checks a checksum header, stores the file atomically with strict permissions, and keeps the newest few of each kind. Jade has a backup tool with status, now and list, but she cannot restore. If you lose the passphrase there is no recovery.

The build is unusual. There is no bundler. A base page is patched by many replacements, and each one's old text must occur exactly once. Zero matches stops the build with MISSING and more than one stops it with AMBIGUOUS, so it never produces a half-patched page.
Feature modules are then injected in a fixed order, and the result is one HTML file.

Testing uses Playwright with headless Chromium plus engine tests, and every feature gets a test. The Android app is built without the Android SDK, using stubs, a dex step, a packaging tool and signing. The repository also states honestly what has not run on a real phone.
That habit of saying what was and was not tested is a good one to copy. You now have the map: use the vault, let Jade work within limits, and extend it with skills, flows and playbooks.
